mcq.section: The second pass: objects as bytes
mcq.prompt: What is the difference between an object's *object representation* and its *value representation*?
choices: The object representation excludes padding; the value representation includes it
The object representation is all sizeof(T) bytes; the value representation is the subset of bits that participate in the value
They are the same thing under two names
The value representation is what memcpy copies; the object representation is what the constructor initialises
mcq.explain: The object representation covers every byte a T occupies, padding included; the value representation is only the bits that carry meaning. Getting the inclusion backwards is the trap, and it matters because padding bytes belong to the object representation while carrying no value — which is why memcmp and byte-hashing misbehave on padded types. memcpy copies the whole object representation, padding and all.

mcq.section: The second pass: objects as bytes
mcq.prompt: Two `struct Quote { char side; int quantity; }` objects have equal `side` and equal `quantity`. What can you say about `std::memcmp(&a, &b, sizeof(Quote)) == 0`?
choices: It is guaranteed true, since all members are equal
It is guaranteed false, since the objects have different addresses
It is true only if both objects were value-initialised with {}
It is not guaranteed either way: the padding bytes between side and quantity can differ
mcq.explain: memcmp compares the entire object representation, so it also compares the three padding bytes, whose contents are not specified by member assignment or ordinary initialisation. Value-initialising both with {} makes it *likely* on mainstream implementations but is still not a guarantee the standard offers — and any later member assignment can leave the padding untouched or clobbered. Compare members, and hash members, not bytes.

mcq.prompt: On a typical x86-64 or ARM64 ABI, what is `sizeof(struct { char side; double price; int quantity; })`?
mcq.explain: side sits at offset 0; price needs 8-byte alignment, so seven padding bytes push it to offset 8; quantity occupies 16–19; then four bytes of tail padding round the total up to a multiple of the struct's 8-byte alignment. 13 is the sum of the member sizes and ignores alignment entirely; 20 forgets the tail padding that keeps array elements aligned.

mcq.prompt: Why must `sizeof(T)` be a multiple of `alignof(T)`?
choices: So that every element of a T[] lands on a correctly aligned address
So that memcpy can use word-sized loads
Because the standard requires sizeof to be a power of two
So that T can be placed in a union with any other type
mcq.explain: Array elements are contiguous with no gaps, so the stride *is* sizeof(T); if the size were not a multiple of the alignment, the second element would be misaligned. That is also why tail padding is repeated inside every element rather than appearing once at the end of the array. sizeof is not required to be a power of two — 24 is a common struct size.

mcq.prompt: What is the useful first-pass rule for reducing accidental padding in a struct?
choices: Declare the smallest members first
Declare members in decreasing order of alignment
Make every member the same width
Add an explicit alignas to each member
mcq.explain: Placing the strictest-aligned members first means every later offset is already suitably aligned, so no interior padding is needed until the very end. Smallest-first is the exact inversion and maximises interior gaps — `char; double; int` costs 24 bytes where `double; int; char` costs 16. The rule is a default, not a law: ABI compatibility and semantic grouping can outrank it, but the padding should then be a deliberate choice.

mcq.prompt: `OrderWide` is 24 bytes with 4 bytes of tail padding, and `OrderWide pair[2];`. What does `pair + 1` point at?
choices: The byte immediately after the last value-carrying member of pair[0]
An address 20 bytes on, since padding is not part of the element
An unspecified address; pointer arithmetic on padded types is implementation-defined
&pair[1], exactly 24 bytes on, because pointer arithmetic scales by sizeof
mcq.explain: Pointer arithmetic always scales by sizeof(T), which includes tail padding, so `pair + 1` and `&pair[1]` are the same address 24 bytes along. Believing that the padding is skipped is what makes people expect a 20-byte stride and then compute wrong offsets by hand. The padding lives inside each element, which is why an array of a badly ordered struct wastes memory once per element.

mcq.section: Empty members cost nothing (if you ask)
mcq.prompt: `struct Policy { Less compare; double price; };` where Less is empty. What does adding `[[no_unique_address]]` to the member change?
choices: It removes the member entirely, so its constructor no longer runs
It makes the member's address equal to the struct's address in all cases
It permits the member to overlap other members' storage, typically taking sizeof from 16 down to 8
It packs the struct, removing padding between all members
mcq.explain: Without the attribute, the empty member needs its own address, so it occupies a byte and then seven bytes of padding align the double — 16 bytes for one double's worth of data. The attribute relaxes the unique-address requirement so the member can overlap, and the struct collapses to 8. The member still exists: its constructor and destructor run, its name participates in overload resolution, and its address is a real subobject address. The attribute is a permission, not a guarantee about layout.

mcq.section: Empty members cost nothing (if you ask)
mcq.prompt: A struct has two `[[no_unique_address]]` members of the *same* empty type, followed by a double. What does the language guarantee?
choices: Both empty members share one address, since they are empty
The two members must have distinct addresses, though either may overlap a member of a different type
The attribute is ignored when two members share a type
The struct is ill-formed
mcq.explain: Two subobjects of the same type must be distinguishable by address, so the implementation cannot collapse both empty members to the same place — one of them will consume a byte. Overlap with the double or with a differently typed empty member is still permitted. This is the same rule that limits the empty-base optimisation when a class inherits the same empty base twice.

mcq.prompt: What does `std::is_trivially_copyable_v<Tick>` license?
choices: Copying a Tick with std::memcpy, and round-tripping its bytes through a char/std::byte buffer and back
Assuming Tick has no padding
Sending a Tick over the network unchanged
Default-initialising a Tick to all zero bits
mcq.explain: Trivial copyability is about the *copy* operation: memcpy between two live Ticks is defined, and so is copying the bytes out to a byte buffer and back, restoring the original value. It says nothing about padding, byte order or floating-point encoding, so it is not a serialisation guarantee — the copied bytes are only meaningful to this ABI. And trivial default construction leaves scalars indeterminate, not zero.

mcq.prompt: Which of these disqualifies a class from being standard-layout?
choices: A user-provided destructor
A member of type double
Being declared with `struct` rather than `class`
Data members split across two different access specifiers
mcq.explain: Standard layout is about C-like organisation, and mixed access control among the non-static data members breaks it — as does a reference member or virtual machinery. A user-provided destructor destroys triviality and trivial copyability, but a class can be standard-layout with one, which is exactly why the chapter refuses to treat the properties as nested categories. `struct` versus `class` only changes the default access, not the layout.

mcq.prompt: `Tick` is trivial. What is the difference between `Tick a;` and `Tick b{};`?
choices: None; both zero-initialise the scalar members
`Tick a;` zero-initialises and `Tick b{};` leaves the members indeterminate
`Tick a;` performs no initialisation, so reading its members is undefined behaviour; `Tick b{};` zero-initialises them
`Tick b{};` is ill-formed for a trivial type
mcq.explain: Trivial default construction means "does nothing", so a's scalar members hold indeterminate values and reading them is undefined behaviour — the debug build that appears to show zeros is proving nothing. The braces request value initialisation, which zero-initialises the scalars. Note also that `std::memset(&a, 0, sizeof a)` is not a portable substitute: all-bits-zero is not required to be a null pointer or a floating-point zero, and it writes the padding too.

mcq.prompt: An interviewer asks whether your wire record is "POD". What is the chapter's recommended answer?
choices: Yes, if it has no virtual functions and no constructors
Retire the label and name the properties the operation actually needs — trivially copyable for byte copying, standard-layout for offsetof and C interop — plus the trait that establishes each
POD is now spelled std::is_trivial_v, so answer with that trait
It depends only on whether the type is an aggregate
mcq.explain: "POD" bundled several independent guarantees under one word and the standard split them apart for exactly that reason. A wire record typically needs both is_trivially_copyable_v (to memcpy the bytes) and is_standard_layout_v (to use offsetof and rely on member order); a type needing only fast relocation may need the first and not the second. The folk test "no virtual functions" is necessary but nowhere near sufficient — mixed access control alone breaks standard layout.

mcq.prompt: `union Number { int integer; float real; }; number.real = 1.0F; return number.integer;` — what is the status in C++?
choices: Undefined behaviour: integer is not the active member
Well-defined, and returns the bit pattern of 1.0F
Implementation-defined, and portable across GCC and Clang
Ill-formed; the union member cannot be read
mcq.explain: Only one union member is alive at a time, and reading an inactive member is undefined behaviour in C++ — C permits this style of reinterpretation with caveats, which is where the habit comes from. The code compiles and usually produces the expected bits at -O0, which is precisely why it is dangerous: the optimiser may assume the inactive member is never read and the behaviour changes after inlining. Use std::bit_cast.

mcq.prompt: `union Message { Add add; Cancel cancel; };` where Add is `{int kind; int quantity;}` and Cancel is `{int kind; std::uint64_t order_id;}`. Add is active. What may be read through `message.cancel`?
choices: Nothing; any access through cancel is undefined behaviour
Everything, since both are standard-layout
Only `kind`, because it is part of the two structs' common initial sequence
`kind` and `order_id`, because the storage is large enough for both
mcq.explain: The common-initial-sequence rule is a narrow, deliberate exception that lets a tagged C-compatible record read its discriminator through either alternative. The sequence here stops at `kind`, because `quantity` and `order_id` are not layout-compatible, so reading `cancel.order_id` while Add is active remains undefined behaviour. The exception exists to support tag inspection, not general punning.

mcq.prompt: A union pun works in the debug build and produces wrong results at -O2. What is the right fix?
choices: Mark the union members volatile
Rewrite it with reinterpret_cast, which is a supported cast
Compile that translation unit at -O0
Replace it with std::bit_cast for equal-size values, or std::memcpy when sizes or storage are dynamic
mcq.explain: The behaviour is undefined, so the -O2 result is not a compiler bug and no amount of flag-tuning makes the source correct. reinterpret_cast is the classic non-fix: it only changes the spelling of the same undefined access. bit_cast and fixed-size memcpy are defined, are the documented tools, and normally compile to the very same register transfer the pun was hoping for.

mcq.prompt: `int values[3]; int* finish = values + 3;` — what is legal to do with `finish`?
choices: Dereference it, since it points inside the array's storage
Compare it, but not dereference it
Neither compare nor dereference it; forming it is already undefined behaviour
Dereference it only if the array is const
mcq.explain: The one-past-the-end pointer is explicitly permitted to be formed and compared — that is what makes the half-open iteration idiom work — but dereferencing it is undefined behaviour because no object lives there. Forming `values + 4`, by contrast, is undefined even without a dereference. A non-array object behaves as an array of length one for this rule.

mcq.prompt: Two `int[4]` arrays happen to be laid out adjacently, so `left + 4` has the same numeric address as `right`. Is `*(left + 4)` a valid read of `right[0]`?
choices: No: the pointer's provenance is the `left` array, so it is one-past-the-end and dereferencing it is undefined regardless of the address bits
Yes, since the addresses are equal and both objects are alive
Yes, provided the arrays are declared in the same translation unit
Only after converting to std::uintptr_t and back
mcq.explain: Provenance is the model: a pointer carries the allocation it was derived from, not just an address, and the source-level array boundary controls what it may access. Physical adjacency is an accident of one run and supplies no extra element. Round-tripping through an integer does not launder the provenance either — optimisers reason about the originating object even when the address bits match.

mcq.prompt: `auto* p = reinterpret_cast<std::uint32_t*>(&some_float); return *p;` — where exactly is the undefined behaviour?
choices: In the reinterpret_cast, which is ill-formed between unrelated pointer types
Nowhere; float and uint32_t have the same size and alignment
In the dereference: the float object is being accessed through a type not in its permitted alias set
In the return, because the value may not be representable
mcq.explain: reinterpret_cast merely computes a pointer value and is perfectly well-formed; the undefined operation is reading the float's stored value through a std::uint32_t lvalue, which the strict-aliasing rule does not permit. Equal size and alignment are irrelevant — the rule is about the accessed type, not the byte count. char, unsigned char and std::byte views are the one-way exception: they can inspect the representation, but casting the same address to uint32_t* does not create a uint32_t there.

mcq.prompt: What does std::bit_cast require of its source and destination types?
choices: That both are standard-layout
That the destination is an integer type
That the source is an aggregate
That they have equal size and both are trivially copyable
mcq.explain: Equal size and trivial copyability are the two requirements, and both are checked at compile time — `std::bit_cast<std::uint64_t>(1.0F)` simply does not compile, which is a far better failure than a silent misread. Standard layout is unrelated; it governs offsetof and C interop, not byte-for-byte value construction. Neither type has to be an integer or an aggregate.

mcq.prompt: What is `std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t>(1.0F)` on an IEEE-754 target?
choices: 1, since bit_cast performs the numeric conversion
The 32-bit encoding of 1.0F, which is a large integer, not 1
Undefined behaviour, because float and uint32_t are unrelated
0, because the mantissa of 1.0F is zero
mcq.explain: bit_cast is a *representation* conversion: it reinterprets the bits, so you get the IEEE-754 encoding of 1.0F (sign 0, biased exponent 127, zero fraction), not the numeric value 1. `static_cast<std::uint32_t>(1.0F)` is the numeric conversion that yields 1 — confusing the two is the whole point of the exercise. The behaviour is fully defined; that is the difference from a reinterpret_cast pun.

mcq.prompt: When should you still reach for std::memcpy instead of std::bit_cast?
choices: When the size is a runtime quantity, or you are copying into storage rather than producing a value
When the types are not trivially copyable, since memcpy relaxes that requirement
When the code must run in a constant expression
When the destination is smaller than the source
mcq.explain: bit_cast produces a value and needs a compile-time-equal size; memcpy handles dynamic lengths and writes into an existing destination object, which is why the wire parser memcpys a whole buffer into a record. Neither tool relaxes trivial copyability. Constant evaluation is the other way round: bit_cast is the one that can be constexpr, memcpy is not.

mcq.prompt: Which statement about byte order is correct?
choices: Little-endian stores the most-significant byte at the lowest address
x86-64 is big-endian and ARM64 is little-endian
Network byte order is big-endian, while mainstream x86-64 and ARM64 hosts are little-endian
std::endian::native is always std::endian::little on a 64-bit host
mcq.explain: Big-endian puts the most-significant byte first and is the traditional network order; both mainstream 64-bit host architectures are little-endian, which is why a byteswap is normally needed at the wire boundary. std::endian::native reports the target's order and is not fixed by word size — the chapter's example static_asserts that it is one of the two known orders rather than assuming little.

mcq.prompt: A big-endian feed carries an IEEE-754 binary32 price. How do you decode it on a little-endian host?
choices: Call std::byteswap on the float directly
Read the four bytes into a std::uint32_t, byteswap that integer, then std::bit_cast it to float
Read it as a float and negate the exponent
Read it as a double, since doubles are endian-neutral
mcq.explain: std::byteswap is defined for integer types only, and "swapping a float numerically" is not a meaningful operation — you must treat the representation as a same-size integer, reverse it, and then reinterpret the bits with bit_cast. This still assumes both ends agree on binary32; endianness conversion cannot bridge different numeric formats. No floating-point type is endian-neutral.

mcq.section: Pinning layout: offsetof and the wire flagship
mcq.prompt: The wire record already asserts `sizeof(MdAddOrder) == 32`. Why assert every member offset as well?
choices: offsetof does not compile without a preceding sizeof assertion
Because sizeof is unreliable for standard-layout types
To make the assertions self-documenting; they add no checking
Because a different ABI could keep the total at 32 while moving padding between fields, producing a silently incompatible layout
mcq.explain: Total size is a weak invariant: interior padding can be redistributed without changing it, and every field after the moved gap then decodes garbage. Asserting each offset — plus a final field that reaches the end — pins the whole map, so an incompatible target fails at build time instead of in a feed handler. offsetof itself is only guaranteed for standard-layout types, which is why the chapter pairs it with is_standard_layout_v.

mcq.section: Pinning layout: offsetof and the wire flagship
mcq.prompt: Why must you not write `const auto* msg = reinterpret_cast<const MdAddOrder*>(buffer.data());` and read through it, even when the record is trivially copyable and standard-layout?
choices: The buffer address may not satisfy MdAddOrder's alignment, and its storage holds byte objects rather than a live MdAddOrder
reinterpret_cast cannot produce a pointer to a class type
It is fine; the trait assertions are exactly what make it legal
It would copy the whole buffer, which is slower than memcpy
mcq.explain: Two independent defects: an arbitrary receive buffer need not be 8-byte aligned, and no MdAddOrder object has ever been created in that storage, so the access is not reading an object of that type. The trait assertions license *copying the bytes* into a real MdAddOrder — which is why the chapter memcpys into a local — not manufacturing one in place. The memcpy is normally optimised into direct loads, so nothing is lost by doing it correctly.

reading.prompt: An audio clip header embeds a format record. What does this print on a 64-bit target?
reading.explain: SampleFormat is 16 bytes: the double fills 0-7, channel_count 8-11, and four bytes of tail padding round the size up to the 8-byte alignment. The tempting answer is that ClipHeader is also 16, because frame_count looks like it should slot into the member subobject's unused bytes 12-15. It cannot: a member subobject occupies its full sizeof, so format spans 0-15 and frame_count starts at offset 16, giving 24 bytes with four more tail bytes. Nesting a struct with tail padding therefore costs the padding twice.

reading.section: Empty members cost nothing (if you ask)
reading.prompt: A physics engine tags bodies with an empty policy type. What does this print?
reading.explain: All three are 8: the attribute lets each empty member overlap storage that the double already occupies, in front of it, behind it, or both. The tempting answer is 8 16 16 — that a member can only overlap what precedes it, so a trailing Tag needs its own byte, and two Tags need two. The layout rule is weaker than that: it only forbids two potentially-overlapping subobjects of the *same type* from sharing one address, and first and second satisfy that by sitting at two different offsets inside the padding-free double. Without the attribute Front would be 16, because the byte for tag drags seven padding bytes behind it.

reading.prompt: A sprite loader wants one integer per pixel. What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: std::bit_cast requires sizeof(From) == sizeof(To), and Rgb is three bytes against four for std::uint32_t, so the call is ill-formed. The tempting reading is that padding rounds Rgb up to four bytes: it does not, because alignof(Rgb) is 1 and no padding is needed. The fix is to state the encoding explicitly (shift the three channels into a uint32_t) or to add a fourth explicit channel byte to the struct so the sizes really do match.

reading.prompt: A sensor feed sends IEEE-754 floats in network order. What does this print?
reading.explain: The four wire bytes 3F C0 00 00 are the big-endian encoding of 1.5f. The bytes are copied into an integer, swapped only on a little-endian host, and then reinterpreted as a float with std::bit_cast, so the round trip back to the integer image reproduces 0x3FC00000 and the comparison is true. The tempting mistake is to byteswap the float itself — there is no numeric swap of a float, and swapping after the bit_cast would produce a different value entirely. Note that the swap is conditional: on a big-endian host the bytes are already in place.

reading.prompt: A window toolkit stores events in a union. What does this print?
reading.explain: Resized is the active member, yet kind and timestamp may be inspected through KeyDown: both structs are standard-layout and their first two members have layout-compatible types, so those two members form the common initial sequence. The sequence stops at the first mismatch, so reading event.key.scancode would be undefined behaviour even though it sits at an offset that exists in both structs — the tempting reading is that "the bytes are there, so any member is readable". Only the matching prefix is guaranteed.

reading.section: Pinning layout: offsetof and the wire flagship
reading.prompt: A parser skips a one-byte frame marker before reading a header. What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: frame + 1 is not a multiple of alignof(Header), and there is no Header object living in those bytes, so the member access has undefined behaviour on two counts: misaligned access and access through a type that cannot alias an array of std::byte. The tempting reading is that x86 tolerates unaligned loads so the code is merely slow; tolerance of the instruction is not permission from the language, and the sanitizer reports the misaligned member access. Copy the bytes into a Header with std::memcpy instead — the copy is defined at any offset and normally compiles to the same loads.

reading.prompt: A tile map keeps two rows as separate arrays. What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: cursor is a valid one-past-the-end pointer for upper, but every dereference through it leaves that array. Physical adjacency of the two locals grants nothing: the pointer's provenance is upper, so the reads are out of bounds and the sanitizer reports a stack overflow. The tempting reading is that the two arrays are laid out back to back so the loop simply sums lower — the compiler is free to reorder, pad, or keep lower in registers, and it may assume the loop stays inside upper. A tile map that needs one flat address space must allocate one array and index into it.

reading.prompt: Three record types from a glyph cache. What does this print?
reading.explain: The two properties are largely independent, which is exactly what this prints. GlyphKey mixes public and private data members, so it is not standard-layout, but its copy operations and destructor are still trivial. FrameTimer is the mirror image: a user-provided destructor destroys trivial copyability while the C-like layout survives. SlotRef holds a reference, which disqualifies standard layout but leaves a trivial, non-deleted copy constructor, so it remains trivially copyable. The tempting reading is that these are nested categories where one failure implies the other; asking for the exact property the operation needs is the only reliable test.

writing.section: The second pass: objects as bytes
writing.prompt: A glyph cache keyed by `struct Glyph { char32_t code; std::uint8_t page; float advance; };` reports intermittent misses on keys that compare equal: the previous hash hashed all `sizeof(Glyph)` bytes. Write `same_glyph` and `glyph_hash` satisfying this contract: two Glyph values whose members are all equal must always produce the same hash, whatever the storage they were built in, and neither function may inspect raw bytes. Add one comment naming the defect in the byte-wise version.
checklist: same_glyph compares the three members and returns bool
glyph_hash combines per-member hashes; no memcpy, memcmp or std::byte view appears
A comment states that the byte-wise hash also hashed padding, whose contents are unspecified
Both functions take const Glyph& and are marked noexcept
writing.notes: The same argument rules out std::memcmp as the equality predicate. A float member adds its own wrinkle: 0.0f and -0.0f compare equal but have different representations, so a byte-wise hash would also break the hash/equality contract for a type with no padding at all. If a canonical byte image is genuinely wanted, define one explicitly with no implicit padding rather than borrowing the ABI layout.

writing.prompt: A particle system stores `struct Particle { bool alive; double x; float mass; std::uint16_t sprite; double y; };` in an array of 100000. Declare `struct ParticleCompact` with the same five members and the same names, reordered so the type is as small as the ABI allows, and pin the result with static_asserts on the size, the alignment, and every member offset. Do not use packing pragmas or attributes.
checklist: All five members are present with unchanged types and names
Members are ordered by non-increasing alignment
static_assert pins sizeof and alignof
static_assert pins offsetof for each of the five members
sizeof(ParticleCompact) is 24, down from 40
writing.notes: The original wastes 16 bytes per particle, 1.6 MB across the array, purely on interior padding. Sorting members by decreasing alignment is a first pass, not a law: ABI compatibility, semantic grouping, or splitting hot from cold fields can outrank it. Pinning offsets rather than only sizeof matters because a later edit can preserve the total while moving a field.

writing.section: Empty members cost nothing (if you ask)
writing.prompt: Write `template <class Compare> class ScoreTable` holding a comparator and a `std::uint32_t count_`. Contract: the comparator must be a member, not a base class; the class must expose `prefers(a, b)` that calls the comparator and `size()`; and `sizeof(ScoreTable<C>)` must be 4 when C is empty and 8 when C carries a `std::uint32_t`. Prove both with static_asserts.
checklist: The comparator is a data member marked [[no_unique_address]]
No inheritance from Compare appears
prefers forwards to the stored comparator; size returns count_
static_assert shows sizeof is 4 for an empty comparator
static_assert shows sizeof is 8 for a comparator holding a std::uint32_t
writing.notes: Without the attribute the empty comparator occupies a byte and drags three more bytes of padding in front of count_, doubling the object. The empty-base optimization would achieve the same saving, at the cost of expressing a storage trick as an is-a relationship and of failing outright if the comparator is marked final. Keep the size assertion next to the class: it turns a future stateful comparator into a visible decision instead of a silent growth.

writing.prompt: `SpriteFrame` is uploaded to a GPU buffer by copying its bytes. Define the type and a tripwire block that fails the build if any future edit breaks the upload: it must assert the exact property the byte copy relies on, assert C-like layout so offsets stay usable, and assert that the record contains no implicit padding by comparing `sizeof` with the sum of member sizes. Then write `void upload(std::span<std::byte> destination, const SpriteFrame& frame)` that copies the record and asserts the destination is large enough.
checklist: static_assert(std::is_trivially_copyable_v<SpriteFrame>) is present
static_assert(std::is_standard_layout_v<SpriteFrame>) is present
A static_assert compares sizeof(SpriteFrame) with the sum of the member sizes
upload uses std::memcpy, not a reinterpret_cast of the destination
upload checks destination.size() before copying
writing.notes: Trivial copyability is the property that licenses the byte copy; standard layout is what keeps offsetof and cross-language field agreement meaningful. The sum-of-sizes assertion is the one that catches a reordering edit: inserting a std::uint8_t between two 16-bit fields would keep both traits true while silently adding a padding byte the GPU side does not expect. None of this makes the record portable across machines — endianness and floating-point format are separate protocol decisions.

writing.prompt: A tile map cell holds either an integer atlas index or a float blend weight. A colleague implemented it as a bare union and reads whichever member the caller asks for. Write `class Cell` that keeps the same storage but makes the active member explicit: a `Kind` enum, `set_index` and `set_weight` that record the new active member, and `index()`/`weight()` that throw `std::logic_error` when the requested member is not active. Add a comment saying why the common-initial-sequence rule does not rescue the original design.
checklist: A union of the two alternatives plus a separate Kind tag member
Each setter assigns its member and updates the tag
Each getter checks the tag and throws when it does not match
A comment explains that reading an inactive member is undefined behaviour
The comment notes that the common-initial-sequence exception applies only to standard-layout struct members with a matching prefix
writing.notes: The tag is the whole point: the union supplies storage, and the class supplies the lifetime bookkeeping the language will not do for a bare union. If the goal were reinterpreting the bits of one member as the other, the tool is std::bit_cast, not a union read. std::variant (Chapter 14) is the standard version of this class when the alternatives need non-trivial construction.

writing.prompt: An audio filter needs a sign test that is exact for negative zero, which `value < 0.0f` misses. Write `constexpr bool has_sign_bit(float value)` and `constexpr float with_sign_bit_cleared(float value)`, each inspecting the representation. Contract: both must be usable in a constant expression — prove it with static_asserts including `has_sign_bit(-0.0f)` — and neither may use a union or a `reinterpret_cast`.
checklist: Both functions are constexpr and use std::bit_cast in both directions
No union member read and no reinterpret_cast appears
static_assert(has_sign_bit(-0.0f)) is present and passes
A static_assert shows that with_sign_bit_cleared(-2.5f) is 2.5f
A static_assert or comment records that the code assumes a 32-bit IEEE-754 float
writing.notes: std::bit_cast is constexpr when both types are trivially copyable and the result holds no indeterminate bits, which is why the same code works at compile time and at run time; std::memcpy would compile but would not be usable in the static_asserts. The remaining assumption is the representation itself: the sign bit is bit 31 only for IEEE-754 binary32, so keep the size assertion beside the functions.

writing.prompt: A telemetry frame carries a 48-bit unsigned timestamp in six big-endian bytes. Write `write_be48(std::span<std::byte, 6>, std::uint64_t)` and `std::uint64_t read_be48(std::span<const std::byte, 6>)`. Contract: the encoder must produce identical bytes on a big-endian and a little-endian host, must touch exactly six bytes, and the pair must round-trip; state what happens to a value that does not fit in 48 bits.
checklist: Both functions work a byte at a time with shifts and masks
Neither calls std::byteswap nor branches on std::endian
Exactly six bytes are written and six read
The most significant byte of the value lands at index 0
The out-of-range case is rejected or documented
writing.notes: std::byteswap is no help here: it reverses all eight bytes of a std::uint64_t, and a 48-bit field is not a whole scalar. Doing the work with shifts on the value keeps the function independent of the host order, which is why no std::endian test appears. The range check matters because a silently truncated timestamp decodes as a plausible wrong time rather than as a failure.

writing.section: Pinning layout: offsetof and the wire flagship
writing.prompt: A map-streaming protocol sends a 24-byte chunk header: chunk id (u64), tile count (u32), checksum (u32), layer (u16), compression (1 byte), flags (1 byte), payload length (u32); all multi-byte fields are big-endian. Define the record so no implicit padding exists, pin size, alignment and every offset with static_asserts, and write `ChunkHeader parse_chunk(std::span<const std::byte>)` that rejects a short buffer and converts every multi-byte field. Do not obtain the record by casting the buffer pointer.
checklist: Members are ordered so every field is naturally aligned with no implicit padding
static_asserts pin trivial copyability, standard layout, sizeof, alignof and all seven offsets
parse_chunk checks buffer.size() before touching the bytes
The record is filled with std::memcpy, never a reinterpret_cast of buffer.data()
Every multi-byte field is byteswapped only on a little-endian host
writing.notes: The single-byte compression and flags fields need no conversion, and placing them at offsets 18 and 19 is what keeps payload_length naturally aligned at 20 without an implicit gap. Copying into the local record is the load-bearing step: buffer.data() may be misaligned and its bytes are std::byte objects, not a live ChunkHeader, so a cast-and-dereference would be undefined behaviour even where the hardware would tolerate the load. Compilers normally turn the fixed-size memcpy into the same instructions the cast would have produced.
